1: Christopher Marlowe (1564–1593) was an English playwright and poet of the Elizabethan stage, Shakespeare's exact contemporary. Doctor Faustus dramatizes a German scholar who bargains his soul for forbidden knowledge and power.
2: Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712–1778) was a Geneva-born philosopher of the French Enlightenment. The Creed of a Savoyard Priest, a section of his book on education, Émile, presents a humble country priest setting out his personal faith drawn from nature and conscience.
3: William Harvey (1578–1657) was an English physician to the kings of England. On the Motion of the Heart and Blood is the treatise in which he reports the experiments and reasoning behind his account of how blood moves through the body.
4: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (1749–1832) was Germany's greatest writer, a poet, dramatist, and statesman. Egmont is his tragedy set in the sixteenth-century Netherlands under Spanish rule, centered on a popular nobleman caught between his people and their rulers.
5: Adam Smith (1723–1790) was a Scottish moral philosopher regarded as the founder of modern economics. The Wealth of Nations is his sweeping study of how nations produce and distribute wealth; this passage takes up the rent of land.
6: Richard Henry Dana Jr. (1815–1882) was a young Harvard man who shipped out as a common sailor and later became a lawyer. Two Years Before the Mast is his vivid memoir of life at sea on the voyage around Cape Horn.
7: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) is the English playwright and poet widely held the greatest in the language. Hamlet follows the Prince of Denmark after his father's death and his mother's hasty remarriage; these scenes belong to its later acts.
8: John Woolman (1720–1772) was an American Quaker, tailor, and travelling preacher. The Journal of John Woolman records his inward life and his early labors against slavery and injustice.
9: The Psalms are the book of sacred songs and prayers at the heart of the Hebrew Bible, long ascribed in part to King David. This selection gathers several of them.
10: Sophocles (c. 496–406 B.C.) was one of the three great tragedians of ancient Athens. Oedipus the King opens on a plague-stricken Thebes, as its ruler Oedipus vows to hunt down the cause of the city's suffering.
11: Edmund Spenser (c. 1552–1599) was an English poet of the Elizabethan age, author of The Faerie Queene. The Epithalamion is the wedding song he wrote to celebrate his own marriage, following the day from dawn to nightfall.
12: The Bhagavad-Gita is a revered Hindu scripture, a dialogue set within the great Sanskrit epic the Mahabharata. On the eve of battle, the warrior Arjuna takes counsel with the god Krishna.
13: Plutarch (c. A.D. 46–120) was a Greek biographer of the Roman era, famous for his paired Lives of great Greeks and Romans. His Life of Aristides portrays the Athenian statesman renowned for his fairness.
14: Plato (c. 428–348 B.C.) was the Athenian philosopher and pupil of Socrates. Crito is a short dialogue in which a friend visits the condemned Socrates in his prison cell and urges him to escape.
15: Jean Froissart (c. 1337–c. 1405) was a French chronicler of the Hundred Years' War. His Chronicles record the events of fourteenth-century Europe; this passage recounts the great English peasants' rising led by Wat Tyler.
16: Lord Byron (1788–1824) was an English Romantic poet and a celebrity of his age. Manfred is his dramatic poem set among the high peaks of the Alps, where a tormented nobleman summons the spirits of the earth.
17: John Eliot (1604–1690), the “Apostle to the Indians,” was a Puritan missionary in colonial Massachusetts. His Brief Narrative reports to England on his work and travels among the Native peoples of New England.
18: Jacob Grimm (1785–1863), with his brother Wilhelm, collected the German folk tales known as Grimms' Fairy Tales. This is their version of the old story of Cinderella, the mistreated daughter and her night at the ball.
19: Raphael Holinshed (c. 1525–1580) compiled the great Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland that Shakespeare later mined for his history plays. This curious passage describes the dogs of England and their kinds.
20: Charles Darwin (1809–1882) was the English naturalist whose later work transformed biology. The Voyage of the Beagle is the journal of his five-year survey expedition; here he observes the wildlife of distant coasts.
21: John Ruskin (1819–1900) was the most influential English art and social critic of the Victorian age. Sesame and Lilies collects his lectures; this one, on books and reading, asks what it means to read well.
22: Pliny the Younger (c. A.D. 61–113) was a Roman lawyer and administrator under the emperor Trajan. His Letters give a vivid picture of Roman life; here he passes on a few tales of the supernatural.
23: John Stuart Mill (1806–1873) was a British philosopher and economist, a leading liberal thinker of the nineteenth century. His Autobiography describes the extraordinary, rigorous education his father gave him from earliest childhood.
24: The Thousand and One Nights (the Arabian Nights) is a great medieval collection of Middle Eastern and South Asian tales, told within the frame of Scheherazade's nightly storytelling.
25: Robert Herrick (1591–1674) was an English clergyman and one of the “Cavalier poets.” Hesperides is his book of short, graceful lyrics on country life, love, and the swift passing of time.
26: Beowulf is the great heroic poem of the Anglo-Saxons, the oldest surviving epic in English, composed by an unknown poet. It tells of the warrior Beowulf and the monsters he is called to face.
27: Francis Bacon (1561–1626) was an English statesman and philosopher who championed the new experimental science. His Essays are brief, pointed reflections on worldly matters; this selection takes up a handful of them.
28: Charles Darwin (1809–1882) was the English naturalist whose later work transformed biology. The Voyage of the Beagle is the journal of his five-year survey expedition; here he records the people and customs of South America.
29: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) is the English playwright and poet widely held the greatest in the language. Macbeth follows a Scottish general who, spurred by a prophecy and his wife, turns his thoughts toward the throne.
30: John Stuart Mill (1806–1873) was a British philosopher and economist, a leading liberal thinker of the nineteenth century. On Liberty is his essay on the proper limits of the power society may exercise over the individual.
